prs.title: test(oxlint): use code that fails to parse regardless of source type
feat(lexer): introduce SIMD vector types
prs.author: overlookmotel
prs.body:
Introduce SIMD vector types `Vec256` and `Vec128`.

These types wrap `__m256i` / `__m128i` on x86_64, and `uint8x16_t` / `uint8x16x2_t` on aarch64.

Motivation:

1. Provide safe interface for operations which are not inherently unsafe e.g. XOR-ing 2 vectors.
2. Provide safe methods for loads from slices (which we can hopefully make more use of in future).
3. Make it impossible to use AVX2-specific intrinsics unless on a machine which supports AVX2, by requiring an `Avx2` token for any methods which create vectors.
4. Make SIMD code less verbose and more readable, by supporting e.g. `vec1 & vec2` or `vec & 0x3F`.
5. A step towards removing all `#[cfg]` feature gates from the crate.

Migrate all the SIMD code in the crate over to using these types.

This is pure refactor. Codegen (ASM) is identical after this PR. The new types express the exact same operations, just through a different syntax.

Any function that receives a `Vec256<Avx2>` / `Vec128<Avx2>` no longer needs to also receive an `Avx2` token - receiving the vector type proves the machine supports AVX2, as it's impossible to create one without providing an `Avx2` token originally.

Some previously unsafe functions become safe, after this change.

prs.title: refactor(lexer): `cpu_version` macro wrap safe functions so they remain safe
prs.author: overlookmotel
prs.body:
Part of effort to move to runtime CPU feature detection.

Safe functions that have a `#[target_feature]` attribute require an `unsafe { ... }` block to call. Such functions also receive an `Avx2` / `Neon` token as a parameter, which proves that the function is safe to call.

Make the `cpu_version` macro wrap such functions so that they maintain their safe interface, and calling them no longer requires an `unsafe { ... }` block. The macro checks the `Avx2` / `Neon` token is present.

prs.title: refactor(lexer): convert `cpu_version` and `cpu_versions` macros to proc macros
prs.author: overlookmotel
prs.body:
Part of effort to move to runtime CPU feature detection.

The `cpu_version` and `cpu_versions` macros had become unweildly, and we'd reached the edge of what it's possible to do with declarative macros, even using all the tt-muncher tricks. Some improvements were impractical to make.

Convert both macros to proc macros in a new `oxc_lexer_macros` crate.

The proc macros are half as many lines of code, easier to understand, and more capable.

This also allows getting rid of the weird `apply` wrapper:

```rust
// Before
#[apply(cpu_version(Avx2))]
// After
#[cpu_version(Avx2)]
```

Rename `cpu_versions` to `cpu_multiversion`, which describes it better.

prs.title: refactor(lexer): `cpu_version` and `cpu_multiversion` macros support associated functions that use `Self`
prs.author: overlookmotel
prs.body:
Part of effort to move to runtime CPU feature detection.

The `cpu_version` and `cpu_multiversion` macros previously could not identify associated functions (methods) of types which don't receive a `self` param. Fix this by also searching the tokens of the function for `Self`.

Switch some functions back to using `Self` where previously they couldn't due to the shortcomings of the macros.

prs.title: perf(lexer): speed up macros
prs.author: overlookmotel
prs.body:
Part of effort to move to runtime CPU feature detection. Follow-on after #28681.

Speed up the proc macros that PR introduced, by reducing `syn` usage. By not parsing the bodies of functions, the compile-time cost of the macros is reduced by 2x.

prs.title: fix(lexer): macros place attributes on correct functions
prs.author: overlookmotel
prs.body: Fix how the `cpu_version` and `cpu_multiversion` macros handle attributes on the function. Apply those attributes either to the dispatcher function or the implementation function, depending on their type.

prs.title: fix(lexer): `cpu_version` macro always validate proof param
prs.author: overlookmotel
prs.body:
`cpu_version` macro passes through the function unchanged where the function is unsafe or has an `#[inline(always)]` attribute. It checks that the function has an appropriate param which proves that the system supports the required CPU features (e.g. `cpu: Avx2` param for a function marked `#[cpu_version(Avx2)]`.

However, that check is based on the source text only. The macro can only see the name of the type in the param, not it's actual type. Add a line to the body of the function that checks the proof - making sure the type passed in is what it appears to be e.g.:

```rust
let _: crate::cpu::Avx2 = cpu;
```

prs.title: refactor(lexer): add `#[cpu_version(Generic)]` to all singly-compiled functions
prs.author: overlookmotel
prs.body:
Add `#[cpu_version(Generic)]` attribute to every function which is not compiled for every possible CPU feature set.

This has little effect - the macro doesn't alter the function - but it does check the function receives no params which suggest it should be compiled for a specific CPU feature set (e.g. `cpu: Avx2`), and makes it clear which paths through the code are intentionally not compiled twice for AVX2 and generic.

After this PR, every function that is part of the pipeline is marked with either `#[cpu_version]` or `#[cpu_multiversion]`.

prs.title: docs(lexer): document functions not called at runtime
docs(skills): guide migrate-oxfmt to check known divergences
refactor(lexer): update `#[inline]` attrs to preserve original inlining
prs.author: overlookmotel
prs.body:
Part of effort to move to runtime CPU feature detection.

Most of this stack has been converting to a pattern where the crate is compiled twice for different CPU feature sets - AVX2 and generic.

In the process, a few changes occured to the ASM, resulting from different inlining decisions.

Adjust inlining to bring the codegen for AVX2 back to as close as possible to what it was before all these changes.

fix(codegen): preserve names in duplicate source mappings
prs.author: camc314
prs.body:
When an unnamed parent node and a mangled identifier begin at the same source position, codegen deduplicated the identifier mapping. This retained location data but discarded the original identifier name, leaving consumers unable to restore inferred function names in source-mapped Node stack traces. ```mermaid flowchart LR A[AssignmentExpression mapping
unnamed] --> B[Token at source position P
name: none] C[Identifier mapping
name: longName] --> D{Same source position P?} D -->|before| E[Drop duplicate
names: empty] D -->|after| F[Enrich existing token
name: longName] ``` ### Changes - Cache whether the last emitted token has a name, keeping duplicate-position handling cheap in the source-map builder hot path. - Enrich an unnamed duplicate token when a later identifier mapping supplies the original name. - Add a unit regression test for the builder behavior. - Extend the existing Node source-map stack-trace snapshot test with a mangled ES module fixture. The Node fixture verifies: ```text function longFunctionName(longName) { ... } ↓ mangled function e(e) { ... } ``` and asserts that the source map includes both original names while Node restores the inferred inner frame as: ```text at longName (/project/input.js:6:15) ```

prs.title: fix(semantic): keep block type bindings separate from hoisted vars
prs.author: magurotuna
prs.body:
Fixes #28600.

`var I; interface I {}` in a nested block merged the interface into the hoisted `var`, so the type moved out of the block. TypeScript keeps the interface in the block. #27936 fixed the opposite order, `interface I {} var I;`.

## Cause

Hoisting a `var` records it in `hoisting_variables` for each intermediate scope. `check_redeclaration` falls back to that map, and `declare_symbol_on_scope` then reused the returned symbol, even for a type declaration.

## Changes

- `declare_symbol_on_scope`: a declaration with no value flags only reuses a symbol bound in the target scope. Otherwise it creates a new symbol there.
- `check_redeclaration`: a binding in the scope and a hoisted `var` are now checked separately. Without this, the block's type binding would hide the conflict and the first change would lose the error in `{ var X; interface X {} let X; }`.
- `check_redeclaration`: only the value flags of a hoisted symbol are compared. The symbol can also carry type flags from a declaration in the outer scope, and those do not conflict with a declaration in the block.

The second change also fixes a missed error in `{ interface X {} var X; let X; }`. tsc rejects both forms with TS2481.

The value-flag restriction also fixes a false error on main: `type X = number; { var X = 0; interface X {} }` was reported as a redeclaration, but tsc accepts it.

An uninstantiated `namespace` in a block also has no value flags, so it now gets its own block symbol too. tsc already rejec
…(truncated)

prs.title: fix(minifier): keep array concat chain reads before later side effects
prs.author: Dunqing
prs.body:
Each call in an array `concat` chain reads its arguments before the next call evaluates its own. Merging the calls moves those reads later, so a later argument can change an earlier one first:

```js
function f(arr) { return [].concat(arr).concat(arr.pop()); }
```

With `arr = [1, 2, 3]` this returns `[1, 2, 3, 3]`, but main merges it into `[].concat(arr, arr.pop())`, which returns `[1, 2, 3]`.

A chain now merges only when no later call has an argument with side effects after an earlier call has an argument that `concat` may read. Primitives and array literals don't count as reads. This is the array half of #27580; the string half landed in #27098.

When the merge is refused, the innermost call still folds its leading literals into its array: `[1].concat(1, arr).concat(arr.pop())` → `[1, 1].concat(arr).concat(arr.pop())`.

## Size

`echarts.js` grows by 8 B minified and 6 B gzipped; nothing else in `minsize` changes. The chain `[].concat(ecIns._componentsViews).concat(ecIns._chartsViews)` no longer merges, because with the default `propertyReadSideEffects` a getter on `_chartsViews` could change `_componentsViews`. With `propertyReadSideEffects: false` it merges as before.

monitor-oxc: 48 files larger (+960 B raw, +76 B gzip), 8 B per `concat` call that no longer merges.

## Not covered

With `propertyWriteSideEffects: false`, `arr[0] = 9` counts as free of side effects, so `[].concat(arr).concat(arr[0] = 9)` still merges. The string guard has the same gap; it needs a separ
…(truncated)

prs.author: magurotuna

fix(linter/eslint/no-misleading-character-class): detect more combining characters
prs.author: Sysix
prs.body:
fixes https://github.com/oxc-project/oxc/issues/28729

Generated by Claude Sonnet 5.5 🤖

The upstream rules uses regex to detect if it is a combining character with the `\p` shorthand:
https://github.com/eslint/eslint/blob/main/lib/rules/utils/unicode/is-combining-character.js#L11

Because there is no similar utility in rust, we currently have a self-managed list of character detection.
This list now get extended to detect more characters for other languages like Arabic, Hebrew, Thai ...

Verified manually that the failing test cases also fails upstream.
Did not verfify if the list is really valid and covers all possible combining characters.
I hope that the AI did no mistakes and included characters which are still valid.

prs.title: fix(parser): treat escaped contextual keywords as names, not modifiers
prs.author: d3lm
prs.body:
Treat contextual keywords spelled with a Unicode escape (`st\u0061tic`, `\u0061sync`, `g\u0065t`, …) as property names rather than modifiers. Such a token is an IdentifierName and cannot match a keyword terminal, so `class A { st\u0061tic
 x }` declares two fields named `static` and `x`. Previously it was parsed as `static x` and reported "Keywords cannot contain escape characters".

`try_parse_modifier` and `parse_contextual_modifier` now skip escaped tokens. Invalid forms such as `class X { st\u0061tic y() {} }` are still rejected. The error is now reported at the token after the name, as Babel does, which accounts for the updated parser snapshots.

The new `misc/pass` fixture covers fields named `static`, `async`, `get`, `set`, and `accessor` that end at a line break. The rejected forms are already covered by Babel and test262.

Validated with scoped Rust checks and full parser conformance.

prs.title: fix(linter/unicorn/no-zero-fractions): preserve exponent case
prs.author: camc314
prs.body:
Trim trailing zeros from the fractional part while preserving the exponent suffix verbatim. This avoids false positives on literals such as `4.6566128731E+100` and fixes `1.0E+10` to `1E+10`, matching Unicorn 62.

Fixes #28743

prs.title: fix(oxlint): prevent --init from overwriting existing configs
prs.author: camc314
prs.body:
`oxlint --init` now exits with an error if any supported config filename already exists in the current directory, preserving existing configs and avoiding conflicting ones. Exclusive file creation also prevents overwrites if `.oxlintrc.json` appears after the check.

Fixes #28741

prs.title: fix(linter/eslint/prefer-spread): report calls on non-member expressions
prs.author: camc314
prs.body:
`prefer-spread` now reports `(c ? a : b).apply(null, args)` and `m!.apply(null, args)`, matching ESLint. Check whether the applied expression is a member expression rather than requiring an identifier, while retaining receiver checks for method calls.

Fixes #28728

prs.title: fix(linter/eslint/no-fallthrough): ignore unreachable exits from infinite loops
prs.author: camc314
prs.body:
Cases ending in `while (true)`, `do ... while (true)`, or `for (;;)` cannot fall through unless a reachable break exits the loop. Oxlint reports these cases even though ESLint accepts them.

Traverse CFG edges within each switch and skip the normal exit from statically true loop conditions. Preserve reachable break paths and unused fallthrough comment diagnostics, with regression coverage for async polling, nested breaks, parenthesized conditions, and unreachable breaks.

Linter tests and lint pass. The broader Oxlint suite fails in type-aware suppression tests: one produces different suppression counts, and another aborts because its expected suppression file is missing.

Fixes #28579

prs.title: fix(react-compiler): avoid panic on non-ASCII ref-like names
prs.author: camc314
prs.body:
Reading `object_name[..1]` panics when a ref-like identifier starts with a multibyte character, such as `한글Ref`. Use `.chars().next()` to preserve the ASCII name check without slicing through a UTF-8 character. Ports the fix and regression fixture from https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/38025.

Fixes #28278.

prs.title: fix(linter/unicorn/prefer-single-call): remove duplicate fix status
prs.author: baevm
prs.body:
Noticed that `unicorn/prefer-single-call` rule declared both `pending` and `fix` as its fix status, this PR removes `pending` and also changes to `fix` to `conditional_fix` since the fix is skipped in 2 cases.

Also small change to `declare_oxc_lint` so that it rejects a second fix capability

prs.title: feat(lexer): introduce aligned `VecData` types
prs.author: overlookmotel
prs.body:
Introduce `VecData128` and `VecData256` types, in `simd/data.rs`.

They're byte arrays aligned on 16 and 32 bytes, for lookup tables and other data which is read into SIMD vectors.

- `Vec128::read` / `Vec256::read` read one into a vector, with an aligned load.
- `Vec128::write` / `Vec256::write` write a vector into one, with an aligned store.
- `VecData128::read(cpu)` / `VecData256::read(cpu)` are the same as `Vec128::read` / `Vec256::read`, but read better for tables, e.g. `PH_A.read(cpu)`.

Convert the lookup tables which SIMD code reads into vectors: `PH_A`, `PH_B`, `PH_T`, `MERGED_LUTS`, `WORD_LUTS`, `BITS` (Neon), `QCOMPACT` and `BCOMPACT`.

The aligned read and store operations have minimal advantage over their unaligned versions. The realbenefit is ensuring that loads/stores do not touch multiple cache lines, which has a perf cost.

The change to aligned types has a positive impact for `QCOMPACT` and `BCOMPACT`, which were previously under-aligned, so reads could cross cache lines. Now that they're made up of aligned `VecData256` / `VecData128` blocks, every load is guaranteed to be within a single cache line.

`VecData128::read` and `VecData256::read` are generic over the CPU type. To support that, `CpuSimd` gets `Vec128` and `Vec256` associated types, and there are new `Vec128Impl` and `Vec256Impl` traits, which only contain `read` for now.

feat(lexer): compile all code on all platforms
prs.author: overlookmotel
prs.body:
Remove all `#[cfg(target_arch = ...)]` attributes from the lexer, except in the `cpu` and `simd` modules.

The code for every CPU feature set (AVX2, Neon and generic) is now compiled, type-checked and linted on every platform, including the tests. Rust Analyzer sees all of the code for all platforms "as one". So e.g. AVX2 code can be worked on with full IDE support on an ARM Mac, and `cargo check` / `cargo clippy` on either kind of machine catches errors in the code for the other.

Code for a feature set which the platform doesn't have still can't run, because that feature set's type is uninhabited there (see #28769). The compiler removes it.

The macros change to support this:

- `#[cpu_version]` no longer adds `#[cfg(target_arch = ...)]`. Its `#[target_feature(...)]` becomes `#[cfg_attr(target_arch = ..., target_feature(...))]`, because enabling another platform's target features is an error.
- `#[cpu_multiversion]` generates all 3 entry points (`__avx2`, `__neon` and `__generic`) on every platform, with their target features in a `cfg_attr` in the same way.
- `cpu_select!` compiles all 3 arms on every platform, instead of replacing the bodies of other platforms' arms with `unreachable!()`.

On a platform where a feature set's type is uninhabited, its `#[cpu_multiversion]` entry point starts with `unreachable!()`, before it calls the function body:

```rust
#[inline(never)]
#[cfg_attr(target_arch = "aarch64", target_feature(enable = "neon"))]
#[allow(unreachable_code)]
unsa
